They described a randomized O(n)-query e algorithm for finding global minimum cuts and an O(n e 5/3 )-query algorithm for s, t-minimum cuts in unweighted graphs. context: Linearity allows us to resolve the aforementioned ambiguities in hyperedge reconstruction. For instance, if both {x, y, z} and {x, y, z ′ } appear in cuts, linearity ensures that they are part of the same hyperedge. This observation helps us bypass the need for even cardinality or bounded rank. There is one caveat of 3-hyperedges: there exist two distinct linear hypergraphs (see Appendix A) with 3-hyperedges which have the same CUT-query profile. Fortunately, for the purpose of sparse k-certificates, we can replace 3-hyperedges with cut-equivalent sets of 2-edges, thus preserving correctness for our goal. Related Works Starting with the work of Rubinstein et al. [34], there has been significant interest in CUT-query models for graphs. They described a randomized O(n)-query e algorithm for finding global minimum cuts and an O(n e 5/3 )-query algorithm for s, t-minimum cuts in unweighted graphs. Mukhopadhyay and Nanongkai [30] later generalized Karger’s near-linear time algorithm to provide a randomized O(n)-query e algorithm for global minimum cuts in weighted graphs. Apers et al. [3] subsequently removed the log n factor for the unweighted case using random contraction ideas, though it remains open whether this factor can be removed for weighted graphs. For s, t-minimum cuts, the complexity has been iteratively improved from [34] to a e 5/3 ) bound in unweighted graphs [1], and a randomized O(n deterministic O(n e 8/5 ) bound [20]. Concurrently, Kenneth-Mordoch and Krauthgamer [23] study the all-pairs s, t-minimum cut e 7/4 )-query algorithm, which they recently improved [24] to O(n complexity giving a O(n e 3/2 ). However, these methods fail in weighted graphs, where solving the s, t-minimum cut problem in O(n2−c ) queries for any c > 0 remains an outstanding challenge. A primary motivation for these problems is understanding the complexity of symmetric submodular function minimization (SFM). Queyranne [33] initially designed an O(n3 ) combinatorial algorithm for finding non-trivial minimizers. Using the “isolating cuts” framework [28], Chekuri and Quanrud [9] later reduced symmetric SFM to standard SFM. Combined with Jiang’s O(n2 log n) SFM algorithm [19], this implies an O(n e 2 ) bound for the symmetric case. Regarding lower bounds, while deterministic SFM requires Ω(n log n) queries [6], no ω(n) lower bound is currently known for symmetric SFM. Recent literature has also focused on hypergraph sparsification [26, 11, 21, 32, 25]. While standard models assume a list of edges, Chen et al. [12] studied sparsification via CUT queries and established impossibility results due to the identifiability barriers we address.
